steps.observation: Work on this for 30 seconds; do not stop early. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Conceptual overview of a Transformer neural network

1. Big picture  
   A Transformer is an architecture for processing sequences—sentences, code, sound, protein chains—without the recurrency used by RNNs. Instead, every element in the sequence can “look at” every other element in parallel through a mechanism called self-attention. Stacking many layers of this mechanism lets the model discover ever-richer relationships and representations.

2. Tokens → vectors  
   • Raw text is broken into tokens (words, sub-words, or characters).  
   • Each token is mapped to an embedding vector—a point in high-dimensional space that captures semantic information learned during training.

3. Adding position information  
   Since the model no longer processes tokens one-by-one, it needs to know their order. Positional encodings (sine/cosine patterns or learned vectors) are added to the token embeddings so “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” remain distinct.

4. Self-attention: the core operation  
   For every token, the model forms three projections—Query, Key, and Value—via small learned matrices.  
   • Similarity: A token’s Query is dot-multiplied with every Key in the sequence, producing a score that says how relevant each other token is.  
   • Softmax: Scores are normalized to weights that sum to 1.  
   • Weighted sum: The token’s output representation is the weighted sum of all Value vectors, emphasizing important tokens and down-weighting irrelevant ones.  
   Because this is done for all tokens in parallel, the layer captures pairwise relationships across the entire sequence in one shot.

5. Multi-head trick  
   Instead of a single attention calculation, the layer runs several in parallel (“heads”), each with its own projection matrices. Different heads specialize in different types of relations—syntax, coreference, sentiment, etc. Their outputs are concatenated and linearly mixed.

6. Feed-forward sublayer  
   After self-attention, each token passes through the same small two-layer MLP (often called the position-wise feed-forward network) to transform information non-linearly and expand representation capacity.

7. Residual connections and layer normalization  
   • Residual: The input to each sub-component (attention or feed-forward) is added back to its output, letting gradients flow more easily and preserving information.  
   • LayerNorm: A normalization step stabilizes training by scaling and shifting activations to standardized ranges.

8. Stacking layers  
   A real Transformer stacks this Attention → FFN pair N times (e.g., 6 in the original paper, dozens or hundreds in large models). Deeper layers model longer, subtler dependencies.

9. Encoder, decoder, or both  
   • Transformer encoder: Reads the whole sequence and produces contextualized representations (used in BERT-like models for classification or retrieval).  
   • Transformer decoder: Generates sequences step-by-step, masking future tokens so each position can only attend to earlier ones (used in language generation).  
   • Encoder–decoder (full Transformer): Encoder digests the source sequence (e.g., in one language); the decoder attends to both its own earlier outputs and the encoder’s representations (e.g., machine translation in the original paper).

10. Training objective  
   The model is trained end-to-end with gradient descent on tasks like next-token prediction, masked-language modeling, translation, etc. By repeatedly adjusting its weights so that predicted tokens match ground truth, it learns to embed meaning and capture dependencies.

11. Why it works  
   • Parallelism: All tokens processed simultaneously → efficient GPU usage.  
   • Global context: Self-attention lets each token access information from any other token in one hop.  
   • Scalability: Layer stacking, multi-head attention, and large embedding sizes scale well with more compute and data, driving the performance leaps seen in large language models.

12. At inference time  
   For generation, the decoder is fed the prompt, produces probability distributions over the vocabulary, samples or selects the next token, appends it, and repeats—each step re-runs masked self-attention so the new token can attend to the full context built so far.

In essence, a Transformer repeatedly answers the question “Which other parts of the sequence matter for understanding this token?” and refines its internal picture layer by layer, culminating in highly expressive representations that can be used for comprehension, generation, or downstream tasks.
